structure.title: A story to prolong life
structure.text: The frame establishes Scheherazade's nightly narration and the need to leave a listener wanting continuation.

structure.title: Stories within stories
structure.text: Lang's selection moves through embedded accounts and separate adventures. A character can become a storyteller addressing another character's immediate decision.

people.name: Scheherazade
people.text: A vizier's daughter who volunteers to marry a king who kills each bride the morning after, and who survives by telling him a story each night and leaving it unfinished.

people.name: The king
people.text: A sultan so embittered by betrayal that he has decided no wife will see a second morning, until he finds he cannot stop listening.

people.name: Genies
people.text: Spirits of enormous power, bound in lamps, rings and bottles, who can grant a fortune or ruin a life, and keep the strict letter of every bargain.

context.title: Nested narration
context.text: A story can pause while one of its characters tells another. Keep track of the current speaker and the listener being addressed.
context.takeaway: Each telling has an audience and a purpose.

context.title: Lang's selection
context.text: This is a selected English retelling rather than the entire tradition of the Nights. Selection and wording mediate the reader's encounter.
context.takeaway: Avoid treating one edition as the whole tradition.

notice.why: Narration can seek mercy, prove a claim, or delay an action.

notice.text: Track the exact terms of wishes and bargains.
notice.why: Fortunes can turn on what a speaker failed to specify.

opening: A king has made marriage a death sentence, and Scheherazade volunteers to become his next wife. She tells a story and leaves it unfinished at dawn, giving him a reason to postpone her execution. In Andrew Lang's selection, that desperate bargain opens onto merchants, sailors, genies, and fortunes transformed by an incautious wish or an unexpected encounter. Each adventure offers the pleasure on which the storyteller's life depends: the feeling that, whatever else must happen, the next part cannot be missed.
